LAB STEPS
STEP 01

Install fabric-jumpstart

fabric-jumpstart is a catalog browser that deploys full solution templates into your Fabric workspace with a single command. Start by creating a new Fabric workspace and opening a blank notebook.

In a new Fabric Notebook cell
PySpark%pip install fabric-jumpstart
PySparkimport fabric_jumpstart as jumpstart # See all available solution templates jumpstart.list() # Install Spark Monitoring & Optimization jumpstart.install('spark-monitoring-and-optimization')
fabric-jumpstart installing “Spark Monitoring and Optimization” — Est. 3 min
✅
Installation complete — You will see: Installation complete: Spark Monitoring and Optimization
Click Get Started in the output, or navigate manually to your workspace.
ℹ️
What got installed? Three folders: fabric-platform-monitoring/, spark-simulator/, and spark-recommender/ are created in your workspace.
✅
Verify your installation: If successful, you will see the fabric-platform-monitoring folder appear in your Fabric workspace browser:
☐ NameStatusTypeTaskOwner
📁 fabric-platform-monitoring Folder — —
STEP 02

Explore Your Workspace

After installation, your workspace contains notebooks, pipelines, and an environment artifact. The simulator provides 30+ pre-built Spark jobs to generate realistic monitoring data.

spark-monitoring-jumpstart-test workspace — notebooks, pipelines, and vasa-spark-simulator environment

STEP 03

Configure the Setup Notebook

Open fabric-platform-monitoring/setup/Fabric Spark Monitoring Setup.ipynb. This notebook patches the Spark configuration on each environment you specify so event logs flow to Eventstream.

Option A — Bring your own Spark jobs
Python# Add workspace_id and environment_id for each environment to monitor environments = [ # Replace with your actual IDs "workspace_id": "<your-workspace-id>", "environment_id": "<your-env-id>", ]
Option B — Use the Vasa Simulator (recommended for this lab)

Find the environment ID from the URL of the vasa-spark-simulator artifact:

URL Patternhttps://app.powerbi.com/groups/<workspace_id>/sparkenvironments/<environment_id>?experience=power-bi
Pythonenvironments = [ "workspace_id": "06e0264f-55aa-42f7-983d-445e9b51ca3b", "environment_id": "06b3381c-b2e6-429d-a28b-a7b7aa5ef69b", ]

Run all cells. A successful setup prints:

################### UPDATING ENVIRONMENT workspace: 06e0264f-55aa-42f7-983d-445e9b51ca3b Environment: 06b3381c-b2e6-429d-a28b-a7b7aa5ef69b ################### FINISH UPDATING ENVIRONMENT
⚠️
Prerequisite: The Eventstream must be in Running state before Spark jobs can push logs. The installer creates it automatically — verify in the workspace before running jobs.
STEP 04

Run the Vasa Spark Simulator

If you don’t have real Spark jobs, run the Vasa Spark Simulator Pipeline in fabric-platform-monitoring/spark-simulator/. It executes 30+ synthetic jobs across clinical trial, ML training, and ETL workloads to generate rich and varied telemetry.

💡
What is the Vasa Simulator? Built specifically for workshops, it generates statistically realistic Spark patterns including high-skew jobs, OOM-prone workloads, and driver-bottleneck scenarios — so the recommender has interesting patterns to find.

Navigate to the pipeline and click Run:

  • Go to fabric-platform-monitoring → spark-simulator
  • Open Vasa Spark Simulator Pipeline
  • Click Run All
  • Wait ~5–10 min for all 30+ jobs to complete
spark-simulator folder with pipeline, notebooks, and environment
STEP 05

Verify Logs in the KQL Database

Once the simulator completes, Spark event logs flow through Eventstream into the Spark Monitoring Eventhouse. Verify by opening the KQL database and checking the RawLogs table.

KQL Database tree — RawLogs and SparkLens tables visible
Tables populated after simulator run
TableContents
RawLogsRaw Spark event JSON
SparkEventLogsParsed events
SparkMetricsDriver & executor metrics
SparkDerivedTaskMetricsPer-task aggregates
SparkDriverLogsDriver-side logs
SparkExecutorLogsExecutor-side logs
SparkSQLExecutionEventsSQL query execution plans
🔍
Quick validation: In the KQL database run RawLogs | take 10 — if rows appear, real-time ingestion is working correctly.
STEP 06

Run the Spark Recommender Pipeline

The recommender notebook runs SparkLens analysis on every application, scores performance, predicts scaling outcomes using Amdahl’s Law, and writes structured recommendations back to KQL.

  • Navigate to fabric-platform-monitoring/spark-recommender/
  • Run Spark Recommender Pipeline
  • Wait for completion (~3–5 min depending on job count)
  • Verify the following tables appear in the KQL database:
Tables created by the recommender
sparklens_metadatasparklens_summarysparklens_metricssparklens_predictionssparklens_recommendationsfabric_recommendations
✅
Once you can see sparklens_recommendations and fabric_recommendations in the KQL database, you’re ready for the dashboard.
STEP 07

Explore the Real-Time Dashboard

Navigate to Spark Monitoring Dashboard in the fabric-platform-monitoring folder. The dashboard has four pages — explore them in order for the full story.

Configure these filters first

Autoscale Billing for Spark

Set to true if your capacity uses autoscale billing, false otherwise.

Max Capacity CU

Enter your capacity CU value (e.g. 64) to calibrate the vCore usage chart.

Page 1 — Overview

Overview — Runs Per Hour, Top 10 Apps, vCore Usage (30s window)
Overview continued — Top 10 Artifacts by Duration, vCore trend
Autoscale Billing filter — select true or false
Max Capacity CU filter — enter your CU value
APPLICATION RUN DETAILS

Page 2 — Application Run Details

Select an application and set Executor: All to see CPU efficiency, memory utilisation, GC overhead, shuffle overhead, and task duration percentiles.

App Run Details — CPU efficiency, Executor/Driver memory %, GC overhead, Shuffle overhead
APP COMPARISON

Page 3 — App Comparison

Compare two applications side-by-side. Try Clinical Trial Results Original vs Optimized — the task count difference (112 vs 16) tells the whole story.

App Comparison — Original (112 tasks) vs Optimized (16 tasks)
RECOMMENDATIONS

Page 4 — Recommendations

Every application gets a performance score, root cause analysis, and scaling predictions based on Amdahl’s Law.

Recommendations — CRITICAL driver overhead, scaling predictions 1x→4x, Score 60/100 FAIR
🔑
Reading recommendations: 🔴 CRITICAL = fix this first   ⚠ ROOT CAUSE = what is wrong   📊 IMPACT = quantified waste   🔧 FIXES = actionable code changes   📈 PERFORMANCE SUMMARY = score + band (EXCELLENT / GOOD / FAIR / POOR)
STEP 08

Talk to Your Data — Fabric Data Agent

The Fabric Data Agent connects to your Eventhouse KQL database and answers natural language questions about your Spark workloads. No KQL required. This is the magic moment of the workshop.

⚡
Setup: Create a Data Agent in your workspace and connect it to the Spark Monitoring KQL database. It gains access to all sparklens and fabric_recommendations tables automatically.
Try these questions — start broad, then drill down
What are the 5 applications that take the most amount of time?
Analyze application_1773182849715_0001 — is it driver-heavy or executor-heavy?
Will scaling help this application? Show me the predictions table.
Which applications have the highest GC overhead? What should I fix?
Compare the efficiency scores of all applications. Which is the worst performer?
What Fabric-specific configuration issues did you find? List all critical ones.
Is VOrder enabled for this application? Should it be?
Show me all applications where executor efficiency is below 0.5
🎯
Best demo flow: Find a bad app on the Recommendations page, copy its application_id, then ask: “Analyze [id] — is it driver heavy? Will scaling help?” The agent references both the recommendations and predictions tables and synthesises a verdict in seconds.
